explanations.answer: Test how they live and turn back to God
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The writer says, “Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD.” Look at that word "us." He doesn't point at the crowd from the outside. He stands in the line with everybody else, and I love him for it.

explanations.answer: Rebuild the walls and wait for rescue
explanations.explanation: No trowels and no waiting around in this verse. The writer says, “Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD.” Walls are outside work. This call is about looking at their own ways first, and I think that's the harder job.

explanations.answer: Leave the city and start over elsewhere
explanations.explanation: Nobody's packing boxes here. The writer says, “Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD.” The call isn't about a new address. It's about turning back to the LORD, and that's a different trip altogether.

Yes, "sinned." The prayer says, “We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven.” Nobody in that line makes an excuse. I've blamed a cookie sheet for a scorched batch before, but this prayer doesn't blame a thing, just plain honest words.
Waiting is what you do with a timer and a hot oven. The confession says something else: “We have sinned and rebelled…” They aren't waiting in this line. They're owning up to God in heaven.

Rejoicing is a different mood from this one, friend. The people are confessing, “We have sinned and rebelled…” Everything around that line is heavy, with anger, tears and enemies. It's a confession, not a party.

I see why that might sound right, but the verse says the opposite. The people pray, “We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven.” Those are their own words in the prayer. It's a hard thing to say to God, and I think that's why it hits so hard.

That's right, baker. The prayer says, “We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven.” They don't tell God He has already forgiven them. They say the hard part straight, with nothing sugarcoated.

Yes, prayer. The writer says, “You have covered Yourself with a cloud that no prayer can pass through.” That's how he describes it to God. And look at what he does anyway: he keeps on speaking to God, right to the end of the passage.

Clouds and sunlight go together like dough and a warm oven, so I get the guess. But the verse is about something else: “…a cloud that no prayer can pass through.” The writer isn't talking about the weather. He's talking about prayer.

The enemies do show up in this passage, just not in this verse. Here the writer says God has covered Himself with “…a cloud that no prayer can pass through.” That's the thing that can't get through. It's a heavy picture, friend.
Yes. The writer says, “You have made us scum and refuse among the nations.” Ouch. I think those words hurt to write, and he says them anyway. He's honest about how low it got.
Slaves and servants aren't in this verse. The writer says, “You have made us scum and refuse among the nations.” Those words are rougher than the ones you picked. He doesn't soften anything here.
The writer doesn't use "beggars" or "strangers" here. He says, “You have made us scum and refuse among the nations.” That's a much harsher way to say it. I think he's holding nothing back.
It's the other way around, friend. The writer says, “All our enemies open their mouths against us.” Mouths open, not shut. Not one of these foes is described as silent.
That's right. The writer says, “All our enemies open their mouths against us.” These foes aren't quiet. Their mouths are open against his people.

explanations.answer: Until the LORD looks down and sees
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the stopping point. The writer says his eyes overflow “…until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees.” So the tears have an end in view, and it's the LORD seeing. I think that tells you where the writer is looking while he cries.

explanations.answer: Until the foes leave the land
explanations.explanation: The foes leaving isn't the stopping point he names. The writer says his eyes overflow “…until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees.” The end he gives is the LORD looking down, not the enemy's exit.

explanations.answer: Until the city walls go back up
explanations.explanation: Walls and bricks don't come up in this verse. The writer says his eyes overflow “…until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees.” The end he names isn't a building. It's the LORD looking down.

True, and that's the verse word for word: “My eyes bring grief to my soul because of all the daughters of my city.” His grief is tied to the daughters of his city. I think this man carries his whole city with him.

It's actually true, baker. The writer says, “My eyes bring grief to my soul because of all the daughters of my city.” That's right there in verse 51. His grief reaches past himself to the daughters of his city.
Yes, a pit. The writer says, “They dropped me alive into a pit and cast stones upon me.” I think this one hurts. He says it plainly, and that's how we know how deep it went.
No lions in this verse, friend. The writer says, “They dropped me alive into a pit and cast stones upon me.” A pit, and stones on top of it. It's a hard one to read.
There's no fire in this verse. The writer says, “They dropped me alive into a pit and cast stones upon me.” The place is a pit. I think this part is heavy, so I'll keep it simple.
That's right. The writer says, “…I thought I was going to die.” The waters were over his head, and he says what he thought. I think that's about as low as a man can get, and he's honest about it.
Escape isn't what he thought, friend. The writer says, “…I thought I was going to die.” With water over his head, that was the thought. It's a heavy line.
Rest isn't in this verse. The writer says, “…I thought I was going to die.” That's what went through his mind with the waters over his head. I think it was a scary place to be.

explanations.answer: He calls on the LORD's name
explanations.explanation: Yes. The writer says, “I called on Your name, O LORD, out of the depths of the Pit.” He calls from the depths of the Pit, right where he is. That's the part I'd bake into a plaque.
No climbing in this verse. The writer says, “I called on Your name, O LORD, out of the depths of the Pit.” What he does is call. He does it from the depths, right where he is.

explanations.answer: He goes quiet and gives up
explanations.explanation: He does the opposite, friend. The writer says, “I called on Your name, O LORD, out of the depths of the Pit.” From the depths of the Pit, he's calling. Quiet doesn't win this verse.

Yes. The writer says the LORD drew near when he called, and said, “Do not be afraid.” Think about the order. He called first, and the LORD came close. I think that's one of the sweetest lines in the passage.

That isn't what the LORD says in this verse. The writer says the LORD drew near when he called, and said, “Do not be afraid.” Those are the words the LORD gives him. They're short, and they're right on time.
Going home isn't in this verse. The writer says the LORD drew near when he called, and said, “Do not be afraid.” That's the whole message here. The LORD comes near and says it to him.
True. The writer says, “You defend my cause, O Lord; You redeem my life.” Notice how the verse sits right after the LORD drew near. His words here are about what the Lord does.
It's true, baker. The writer says, “You defend my cause, O Lord; You redeem my life.” That's verse 58, right after the LORD drew near. He says the Lord does both.
True. The writer says, “You have seen, O LORD, the wrong done to me; vindicate my cause!” First he says what the LORD has seen. Then he asks. It's all one breath, and I like how plain it is.
It's true, friend. Verse 59 says, “You have seen, O LORD, the wrong done to me; vindicate my cause!” The asking comes right behind the seeing. They're in the same verse.
Yes, in song. The writer says, “…see how they mock me in song.” I bet a tune that's about you is the hardest kind to get out of your head. It's a rough thing to live with.
Not letters, friend. The writer says, “…see how they mock me in song.” They sing it, whether they sit or rise. No stamps needed.
No riddles here. The writer says, “…see how they mock me in song.” Songs are what the enemies use. I think a song that follows you around all day is hard to shake.

That's not what he says, friend. The writer says, “You will pay them back what they deserve, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.” So he doesn't say they go free. He says the LORD will pay them back.
That's right. The writer says, “You will pay them back what they deserve, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.” Going free isn't in his words. He says the LORD will pay them back.

Look close at that last verse, friend. It says, “You will pursue them in anger and exterminate them from under Your heavens, O LORD.” That "them" is his enemies, not his people. Back in verse 43 it was “…pursued us.”

That's right. Verse 43 says, “You have covered Yourself in anger and pursued us…” The very last verse says, “You will pursue them in anger and exterminate them from under Your heavens, O LORD.” The word turned from "us" to "them." His enemies are now the ones pursued.
